newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, Waigel dismiss German petrol-tax hike report.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, Waigel dismiss German petrol-tax hike report.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Monday dismissed a newspaper report that Bonn plans to raise petrol tax but opposition Social Democrats (SPD) may pull the coalition in that direction.

The tabloid Bild Zeitung newspaper said the government planned to increase the petrol tax by 18 pfennigs a litre on July 1, boosting government revenues by 15 billion marks ($8.8 billion), to finance a one percentage point reduction in unemployment contributions.
"That just isn't true," Kohl told reporters as he entered a meeting of Christian Democrat leaders.
Kohl is due to meet SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine on Wednesday in another effort to reach consensus on tax reform issues.
The government is seeking agreement with the SPD because the opposition can block most tax measures through its control of the upper house of parliament.
The timing of the tax reform is critical as Bonn tries to trim its budget deficit to meet the strict entry criteria for European monetary union.
The government proposes to cut income tax rates, giving taxpayers a net 30 billion mark reduction aimed at stimulating investment and the creation of jobs.
But part of the tax cuts would have to be offset by higher indirect taxes such as value-added tax (VAT) or petrol tax.
The plan outlined in Bild would be in line with SPD calls for an "ecological tax reform" to use the tax system to further environmental protection aims.
Bild said a reduction in contributions to unemployment insurance would be a possible concession by the government to the opposition SPD.
Waigel called the report "pure speculation". The government is prepared to agree on a cut in social insurance payments but details have not been set, he said.
SPD manager Franz Muentefering said his party would be willing to allow a rise in petrol tax if it helped cut social contributions. He also said concrete figures had not been set.

The SPD had wanted a two percentage point cut in such payments as a precondition for agreeing to the tax reform plan. It proposed that the cut be financed through a rise in VAT and petrol taxes and a delay in any further cuts in the solidarity tax levied to help finance restructuring in eastern Germany.
Chancellery minister Friedrich Bohl challenged the SPD ahead of Wednesday's talks to present figures on how much it planned to cut taxes.
The issue has not been fully settled within the coalition camp.

Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, also a leading member of Waigel's Christian Social Union, said he would prefer to see VAT increased. A rise in petrol tax would hurt the automobile industry, which is heavily represented in his state.

But Wolfgang Gerhardt, chairman of the Free Democrats, junior partners in Kohl's coalition, said his party opposed any tax increase. The social security system itself must be reformed to finance cuts, he said.
